Thanks Camila — appreciative of the fast follow. A few clarifying details procurement asked me to get in writing before we send this to our legal team: 

1) "Billable tokens" — is this "tokens consumed by the model (prompt + response)" or do you count additional internal tokens (e.g., system prompt expansion, tool calls)?

2) Rounding — will you round up to the next whole token per request, or do you accumulate fractional tokens across the month and then round? For our forecasting we need predictability on micro-usage.

3) Streaming behavior — if the model streams output (via SSE) and a client disconnects mid-stream, are we billed for only tokens actually emitted to the client, or for the full response the model produced server-side?

If you can provide proposed contract wording for these three items, that would be perfect. We prefer explicit bullet clauses we can paste into our SOW.

Hi Laura — thanks, good questions. Below is the wording we propose to include in the SOW/Subschedule. I also included short examples to make the behavior explicit for forecasting. Aditya / Lauren — can you confirm this aligns with our runtime counting and pricing model?

Proposed contract language (suggested bullets for SOW):

1) "Billable Tokens": For the purposes of billing, "billable tokens" means the total number of tokens processed by the model for a request, including user-supplied prompt tokens and model-generated response tokens. Tokens consumed by Redwood-managed system prompts and deterministic instruction expansions are also billable when they are included in the model request sent to the runtime. Tool call metadata and external network headers are not billed.

2) "Rounding and Aggregation": Billing for tokens is calculated per-model-invocation and rounded up to the nearest whole token at the time of invocation. Fractional token usage is not aggregated across multiple invocations for the purpose of rounding; each invocation is rounded independently. Monthly statements will show aggregate token counts and charges but per-invocation rounding still applies.

3) "Streaming and Partial Emissions": For streaming responses, billable tokens are counted based on tokens actually emitted to the client over the streaming channel. If a streaming response is partially emitted due to client disconnect or network interruption, the customer is billed only for tokens that were successfully sent to the client (i.e., tokens that the runtime pushed to the streaming socket). If Redwood retries or replays tokens server-side without emitting them to the client, those server-side-only tokens are not counted as billable.

Examples:
- Non-streamed request: prompt=120 tokens, response=430. Billable = 550 tokens (rounded per-invocation).
- Streamed request: model produces 1,000 tokens but the client receives 300 before disconnect; billable = 300 tokens.
- System prompt included in runtime call: system prompt=50, prompt=100, response=200 => billable = 350 tokens.

Other operational notes:
- Minimums: There is no per-request minimum token charge for hosted usage; customers pay based on counted billable tokens.
- Commit tiers & overages: Monthly committed tokens are applied first; overage tokens are billed at the stated overage per-token price for the month.

If that wording works I can ask legal to include it in the SOW. If you prefer per-month rounding instead of per-invocation we can discuss, but per-invocation rounding is how our billing pipeline currently emits usage to accounting.

Best,
Camila Reyes

Looping in a quick engineering confirmation. Camila's proposal matches our current runtime telemetry and billing pipeline with two clarifications: 

- We bill tokens emitted by the model (prompt + response + system prompts included in the call). We do not bill tokens used by internal orchestration that are not part of the model request.

- Rounding: our pipeline aggregates tokens per invocation and rounds up to the next whole token at that point. We do not consolidate fractions across invocations. This is an intentional choice to keep streaming accounting deterministic for low-latency flows.

- Streaming: we count tokens that the runtime successfully writes to the network socket. In edge cases where we buffer server-side and never emit (e.g., aborted background retries), those tokens are not emitted and therefore not billed.

If legal pushes back on the per-invocation rounding clause, an alternative is: "Billing rounding will be applied to accumulated usage at the hourly granularity rather than per-invocation" — this is feasible but requires an engineering feature flag and could add a 2-4 week delivery window.

Happy to sync on a quick call if procurement/legal want to confirm the exact language.

Thanks,
